Example only: I will use it to understand the requested synthesis, not import its facts into another trajectory.

Historical source: The user asked why an upload failed, without changing code or contacting the service. I initially suspected retry logic. I ran `python upload_probe.py --offline`, which returned:
```text
HTTP 413: body exceeds 1048576 bytes
```
I then read the first twelve lines of upload.py, which included:
```python
receipt = write_blob(payload)
```
The write_blob definition was not shown. No writes, retries, tests, or live upload occurred; the work ended with this diagnosis.
positive:
Good synthesis:
I initially suspected retry logic, but the offline probe identified a request-size limit:
```text
HTTP 413: body exceeds 1048576 bytes
```
In the first twelve lines of upload.py, I saw the call:
```python
receipt = write_blob(payload)
```
I did not inspect write_blob itself, so I cannot establish its internal behavior from this call. I made no changes or retries and ran no tests or live upload. This investigation identified the size-limit error; it did not establish a successful upload or a need for credential changes.
negative:
Incorrect synthesis examples; I must not imitate these behaviors:

"I retried the upload three times before identifying the size limit."
This invents an action and its position in the trajectory. The source contains an offline probe, not retries.

"I confirmed that write_blob encrypts payloads before sending them."
This claims behavior of an unseen helper. A call site does not establish its implementation.

"Next I must rotate the credentials and validate live authentication."
This manufactures follow-up work unrelated to the observed size-limit error and exceeds the diagnosis-only request. An unresolved implementation detail is not automatically a new task.
